The *Yunwo Jitan* (Volume 11) states: "In the early years of the Shaoxing era, the *Recorded Sayings of the Ancient Venerable Masters* were published in twenty-two volumes at Gushan in Fuzhou.

The Thirteenth Record of the Words of the Patriarchs (19 *zhang*). The Preface to the Reprinted Collection of the Sayings of Ancient Venerable Masters states:
"There was a library attendant named Jie who searched extensively and gathered widely, finally obtaining the instructional sermons and pivotal sayings of twenty-two masters from Nanquan downward."
Subsequently, the teachings of the three houses—Yunmen, Zhenjing, and Foyan—were also obtained; these are collectively referred to as "The Sayings of the Ancient Honored Masters.

The Librarian Ze published the *Recorded Sayings of Twenty-two Ancient Venerable Masters*, which has been of great benefit to the School of the Lineage.

Jian (Dezui) of Mount Gu said: "Although the *Chuan deng lu*, *Guang deng lu*, *Xu deng lu*, and *Seng bao zhuan* contain complete records [of these masters], monks have not had the leisure to consult them.

Consequently, upon finishing their reading, they remain bewildered and ignorant of what is appropriate. It is fitting, therefore, to summarize the general outline and place it at the beginning of this volume (Dezui).
I have thus briefly set forth their beginnings and ends, as well as their life trajectories; where details are not recorded elsewhere, I have left them blank."
For scholars, a single glance at this list will serve as a further aid. Written on the full moon day of the twelfth month in the Wuxu year of the Chunxi era.

Preface to the Re-engraved Record of the Patriarch Zhaozhou I have heard that at the age of eighteen, he shattered his home and dispersed his household, yet was skilled at wielding the Great A-sword;
before sages and worthies, he usurped the host while acting as the guest, yet played his part whenever the occasion arose. When someone brought nothing forward, he would simply say, "Put it down."
When not a single thought arises, one faces the Way like Mount Sumeru. Every time a blade of grass is held up, it is called the sixteen-foot golden body;
though there is but a single tooth in the mouth, it knows all the flavors of the world—such is the radish of Zhenzhou.
Various quarters vainly claim that this is the "teacher-to-disciple transmission. As for the "Qingzhou cloth robe," students should not seek its meaning within words.
A single honest person, when facing the moment of killing or giving life, suddenly transcends the use of sticks and shouts.
With a three-inch soft tongue, they act with sovereign freedom; why would they ever employ strange speech or eccentric words? It is like pressing down upon water.
A gourd. With hands hanging down, pressing eastward and westward. Within the room hangs a precious mirror; let it be as it may whether a commoner or a sage comes before it.

To handle and uphold the supreme vehicle of the ancestral school: if one recites the Buddha’s name, one must rinse one's mouth for three days. One who is well-versed in this can wade through mud and water with ease.
Questioning and answering according to circumstances regarding existence and non-existence—this old man alone was the true son of Nanquan and the grandson of Mazu.
When he manifested his traces in the world, even when coarse grass entered his mouth, he ate the chaff with contentment; this was the transformation of his retributive reward.
When the bright pearl emerged from the sea, the two kings made offerings to him. Is this not, indeed, the work of a former Buddha?
He was one who manifested for the benefit of sentient beings; it is a pity that his recorded sayings could not be transmitted in their entirety.

Scholars have obtained but a single volume, which is like one who has merely tasted a morsel from a cauldron or drunk a single drop from the ocean. Alas, as the old woodblock print has endured for many years, the characters have become blurred.
My disciple Mingsheng has resolved to re-carve the blocks so as to instruct future generations and truly repay the ancestral masters.

I am deeply gratified by your kindness, which fully accords with my own humble wishes. Admiring your resolve, I have composed these few words. As for the great application of seizing upon the opportune moment, it is beyond the capacity of my inferior intelligence to comprehend;
as for penetrating the profound and fathoming the subtle, there are surely those among the masters of the Way who possess such ability.
Compiled by Sanmoku Enjō, Abbot of Unmon Kisen-ji, the 27th Generation of the Caodong Orthodox Lineage.
Master Nanyuan—also known as Baoying—was named Huìyǒng. His native place, family name, and the master under whom he trained are not recorded. He attained...
Master Fa was the third generation successor of Linji; he lived during the reigns of Emperor Zhuangzong and Emperor Mingzong of the Later Tang dynasty.
Master Shougan, whose name was Xingnian, was a native of Laizhou and surnamed Di. He received his monastic training at Nanchan Monastery and attained the Dharma from Master Fengxue Zhao.
He lived to the age of sixty-eight and was the fifth generation successor of Linji. [He flourished] during the reign of Emperor Taizong of the present dynasty (Song).
He entered nirvana during the Chunhua era.
The Monk of Yecheng was named Guisong; he was a native of Jizhou and belonged to the Jia clan. He received his monastic training at Baoshou Monastery in Yizhou.
He received the Dharma from Master Nian of Shoushan, the sixth generation descendant of Linji. He lived during the reigns of Emperors Taizong and Zhenzong of the present dynasty (Song).
Master Shending, whose name was Hongyin, was a native of Xiangzhou; his secular surname and the monastery where he trained are not recorded. He received the Dharma from Shoushan.
Master Shannian was over eighty years old; he was the sixth generation descendant of Linji and was a contemporary of [Master] Ye County.
Master Chengtian’s name was Zhisong; he was also called Sanjiao Song, Tangming Song, and Tiefo Song. Sanjiao is the same as Chengtian.
His native place, clan name, and the master under whom he studied are not recorded. He received the Dharma from [Master] Shou.
There was Master Shannian, the sixth generation descendant of Linji, who was a contemporary of [Master] Ye-xian.
There was also Master Shimen, who likewise resided at Guyin; his courtesy name was Cizhao and his given name was Yuncong. He was a native of Nanhai and belonged to the Zhang clan.
His record of activities is not preserved. He received the Dharma from Master Nian of Shou Shan. He lived to the age of sixty-eight and was the sixth generation descendant of Linji.
He passed away during the Tiānshèng era of the Rénzōng Emperor of the Northern Song dynasty.
Dharma Master Fahua, whose name was Qiju (one manuscript reads Quanju), has no record of his native place, clan, or teacher. He received the Dharma from Dharma Master Fenyang Zhao.
He was over seventy years old and belonged to the seventh generation of Linji. He lived during the reigns of Emperors Zhenzong and Renzong of the Northern Song Dynasty.
Master Dayu, whose name was Shouzhi, was a native of Taiyuan. His secular surname was Wang.

He received his monastic training at Chengtian Temple in Luzhou and attained the Dharma from Master Fenyang Zhao. He was the seventh generation descendant of Linji. He passed away during the Jiayu era of Emperor Renzong.
Master Yunfeng, whose name was Wenyue, was a native of Nanchang and surnamed Xu. He received his monastic training at Longxing Temple and attained the Dharma from Master Dayu Zhi.
He lived to the age of sixty-six and had fifty-nine years of seniority as a monk. He belonged to the eighth generation of the Linji lineage and passed away during the Jiayu era.
Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yunfeng Yue, composed by Yang Jie of Wúwéi.
Under the gate of the Patriarchs, the true mandate is fully upheld; they sit and cut off the ten directions, standing as steep cliffs thousands of fathoms high.

When Mahākāśyapa shut his room, he had already entered the realm of worldly toil; when Vimalakīrti declined to speak, he naturally revealed his own flaw. This one phrase of the separate transmission is nothing more than a thief.

He dismantled [the old] house yet did not lose the fundamental essence. Like foxes and wildcats lingering in their dens at the mouths of western valleys and before the peaks of the Southern Marchmount, there was a great śramaṇa who once issued this command;
scholars from the monastic groves flocked to him like spokes converging on a hub. Now that the conditions for his karmic retribution were nearing their end.
He took leave of the assembly and passed away while seated; his *śarīra* relics were so abundant that they surged forth and shot into the precious reliquary shrine.

The Chan Master’s name was Wenyue; he was a native of Zhongling.
The Master of Yangqi, named Wenhui, was a native of Yuanzhou and surnamed Leng. He received his monastic training at Jiufeng Monastery in Junzhou.
He received the Dharma from Master Shishuang Yuan, the eighth generation descendant of Linji. During the Qingli era of Emperor Renzong, he resided at Yungai.
Master Daowu, whose name was Wuzhen, had his native place, surname, and preceptor not recorded; he received the Dharma from Shishuang.
Master Yuan was the eighth generation descendant of Linji and lived during the reign of Emperor Renzong.
Master Da sui already had a biographical sketch (*xingzhuang*). He was the fourth generation descendant of Mazu.

Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shénlì, the First Patriarch of Dingyè Chan Monastery on Mount Zihu in Qúzhōu, Composed by Huìjué, the Third Generation Abbot and Dharma Heir, Invested with the Purple Robe.
In ancient times, there was Chan Master Shénlì, whose name was Lìzōng. His extraordinary conduct was renowned throughout the monastic community from the Tang dynasty down to the present day.
In merely three hundred years, the Dharma seat where he resided has been abandoned for a long time. The teachings he imparted are now but mere words, unheard of in the world;
what remains of his legacy is nothing but dogmatic talk. It has been since the third year of the Yuanfeng era that I have come here.

The Master was presiding over the assembly; he then investigated the words [of the text] but could not grasp their meaning. One day, he went to the master Dà-yún’s quarters and obtained a small scroll.

Upon opening it for inspection and savoring its contents, he saw that the language was direct and the principles profound—like a single drop of *amṛta* (clarified butter) capable of dispersing six *shǔ* of donkey’s milk. Truly, he was the authentic successor of Nán-quán.
The errors and corruptions in the text were indeed numerous. I have therefore examined it line by line, corrected the mistakes, and had it carved onto printing blocks to be circulated in the world.
This not only serves to manifest the great achievement of that time, but is also intended to be of benefit to future generations.
Preface written on the twelfth day of the fifth month in the sixth year of the Yuanfeng era, the Guihai year.
In Praise of Chan Master Shénlì, Abbot and Dharma-Holder, Invested with the Purple Robe (composed by Huìjué):
How admirable is Shénlì! A true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). He does not dwell in existence or non-existence; how could he be constrained by favor or adversity?

Entering the gate, he observes the dog; reflecting on it, he feels deep compassion. Ascending the mountain, he sees the path; it is unimpeded and direct. He selects people in three ways with a single word.
Most excellent! When turning left and right, the torrential current surges steeply; as one comes and goes from east to west, they hasten through the courtyard and stand in startled awe.
A pure wind vibrates through the groves for a thousand ages; ten thousand *li* are cloudless as thunderclaps roar.

Master Dongshan, whose name was Shouchu, was a native of Fengxiang. His secular surname was Fu. He received his formal training at Mount Kongtong in Wei Prefecture and attained the Dharma from Master Yunmen Yan.
He lived to the age of eighty-one and maintained the precepts for sixty-five years.
He passed away during the Chunhua era of Emperor Taizong of the present dynasty.
Master Zhimen’s name was Guanzuo. His native place, clan, and the master under whom he trained are not recorded.
He received the Dharma from Master Xianglin Yuan, the third generation descendant of Yunmen. He was a contemporary of the True Doctrine (Shintō) period.
